title: Quiche Lorraine
subtitle: Open tart of bacon, eggs, and cream
excerpt: A shortcrust pastry case filled with a custard of bacon lardons, eggs, and cream. The classic quiche Lorraine contains no cheese in the filling, the custard alone sets the tart. One of the great savoury tarts of French cooking.
sourceNotes: Quiche Lorraine is from the Lorraine region in north-east France, bordering Germany and Luxembourg, and its name comes from the German Kuchen ('cake'). The original quiche Lorraine, documented in Provençal cookery from the mid-19th century onward, contained no cheese, only egg and cream custard with lardons. The cheese version is a popular variant. Elizabeth David, French Provincial Cooking (1960), gives the no-cheese version as the authentic preparation. Julia Child, Mastering the Art of French Cooking (1961), gives a detailed method.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Quiche Lorraine is best eaten warm or at room temperature on the day it is made. It can be made up to 4 hours ahead and reheated in a 160°C oven for 10 minutes.
recipe.temperatureNote: fan, blind-bake first then 180°C for filling

glossaryTerms.definition: Baking a pastry case without a filling. The pastry is lined with baking paper, filled with baking beans (or uncooked rice), and baked until the base is set. The beans prevent the pastry from puffing. The paper and beans are removed and the case returned to the oven to dry out before the filling goes in.

content.text: The authentic quiche Lorraine contains no cheese, only a custard of eggs and cream with bacon lardons in a blind-baked shortcrust case. The custard sets to a wobbling, just-firm consistency, neither rubbery nor liquid.
the pastry before adding the filling is essential: it prevents a soggy base.

Rub the cold butter into the flour until the mixture resembles coarse breadcrumbs. Add the egg yolk and 2 to 3 tbsp of ice-cold water and bring together into a dough. Do not overwork. Flatten into a disc, wrap, and chill for 30 minutes.

Heat the oven to 190°C fan. Roll the pastry to 3 mm thickness and use it to line the 23 cm tart tin. Trim and chill for 10 minutes. Line with baking paper and fill with baking beans. Blind-bake for 15 minutes.
Remove the paper and beans. Return to the oven for 8 minutes until the base is dry and pale gold. Reduce the oven to 180°C fan.
Fry the lardons over medium heat until crisp. Drain on kitchen paper. Scatter them over the base of the pastry case.
Whisk together the eggs and double cream.
Season with salt, pepper, and a little nutmeg.

Bake at 180°C fan for 25 to 30 minutes until the custard is just set, it should wobble slightly in the centre when the tin is shaken. It will firm as it cools. Allow to rest for 15 minutes before slicing.

items.cause: It was not blind-baked long enough, or the filling was added before the base was fully dry.
items.fix: Always blind-bake until the base is pale gold and dry to the touch. If the base is still soft when the paper and beans come off, return it to the oven for a further 5 minutes before adding the filling.

items.symptom: The custard has set with a slightly curdled texture
items.cause: The oven was too hot, causing the egg proteins in the custard to over-set and tighten.
items.fix: Reduce to 170°C fan and bake for 5 minutes longer. A custard-based filling must cook slowly at low-moderate heat. At higher temperatures, the eggs scramble rather than set silkily.

items.cause: The pastry was not rested in the tin before baking, or was stretched rather than lifted into the case.
items.fix: Always chill the lined tin for at least 10 minutes before blind-baking. When lining the tin, lift the pastry and allow it to drop into the angles rather than pressing it in, pressing stretches the dough, which then contracts during baking.

content.text: Lorraine in north-east France is a region shaped by centuries of conflict on the German-French border; its cooking reflects both traditions. The quiche, from the German Kuchen, is the most famous export of Lorraine's kitchen. The earliest recipes from the region, from the 16th century onward, used bread dough rather than shortcrust as the case. The modern shortcrust version with an egg and cream custard became standard in the 19th century. The cheese version so common in Britain and America is a later modification not recognised by Lorraine cooks as authentic.
